summary: Considers the problems of downgrading X.400 (1988) messages to X.400 (1984) form. The formal rules for downgrading in X.419 were not sufficient for good service, so this document discusses further handling. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Newer mail machines have features older ones cannot read. This paper explains how to trim a new-style message so an old machine can still understand it.

subtitle: How gateways should downgrade X.400 1988 messages and addresses for 1984 systems.

tldr.problem: X.400 (1988) is a superset of X.400 (1984), and the downgrading rules in annexe B of X.419 are not enough where 1984 and 1988 systems coexist.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds rules for addresses (a DDA named X400-88 and a Common name mapping), IPM content type downgrade, and several choices for converting body parts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1328 is Historic. It still shows how the Internet and COSINE communities approached mixed 1984 and 1988 mail.

today: RFC 1328 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 1327 for the address encoding.

sections.title: The Need to Downgrade
sections.content:
The document considers downgrading from X.400(1988) to X.400(1984). Annexe B of X.419 has some rules, but they are not sufficient for an environment with both 1984 and 1988 components, so this document defines extensions. It is not a tutorial.

Since 1988 is a strict superset of 1984, the mapping is one-way. The most important advice is to configure systems to minimise downgrading, and to strenuously avoid using 1984 systems to interconnect 1988 systems. For distribution lists with both kinds of recipients, messages tend to be lowest common denominator.
sections.eli5: New mail systems can do more than old ones, so going to an old one means dropping things. It is best to avoid that where you can.

sections.title: Downgrading Addresses
sections.content:
O/R addresses using 1988-specific features cannot be specified from 1984 systems, and messages from such addresses cannot be transferred into X.400(1984). Two approaches are defined.

The general approach uses a domain defined attribute (DDA) named X400-88, whose value is an std-or encoding of the address as in RFC 1327. It lets a gateway source-route the message and needs no cooperation. If the result is longer than 128 characters, up to three overflow attributes (X400-C1, X400-C2, X400-C3) are used.

The special approach handles the Common Name attribute by downgrading it to the DDA Common, for example CN=Postmaster becomes DD.Common=Postmaster. The downgrade always works, but the gateway cannot always reverse it, so all 1988 MTAs and UAs that interact through such gateways must understand the equivalence.
sections.eli5: Fancy address parts are folded into a plain label the old system can carry, so the message can still be sent and answered.

sections.title: MTS and IPM Downgrading
sections.content:
For the message transfer system, annexe B of X.419 is sufficient apart from addressing. Discarding envelope fields is unfortunate, but the criticality mechanism ensures nothing the originator marked critical is discarded.

The 1984 IPM service usually uses content type 2, so a gateway may downgrade P2 from content type 22 to 2, depending on configuration and destination. When it does, it strips 1988-specific headings (language indication and partial message indication), downgrades all O/R addresses, and appends any directory name as text in round brackets to the Free Form Name, preferably in the User Friendly Name syntax. A message that originated from RFC 822 can be downgraded better, as discussed in RFC 1327.
sections.eli5: The gateway removes the new-style headings and tucks the sender's full name into brackets so people can still read it.

sections.title: Body Part Downgrading
sections.content:
Body part conversion should be avoided where possible. The options are to downgrade to a standard 1984 body part without or with loss of information, to replace the body part with a text message (for example saying a hologram could not be converted), or to bounce the message.

If conversion is prohibited, the message must bounce. If conversion-with-loss is prohibited, a lossless downgrade should be used if possible, otherwise bounce. Otherwise a lossy downgrade is done if possible, and a choice between the text replacement and bouncing is a configuration choice. Another option is to encapsulate the body part as a Nationally Defined 1984 body part (body part 7) when configured for the recipient UA.
sections.eli5: If a part cannot be turned into something the old system understands, the gateway can swap in a note saying so, or send the message back.
